slides.title: Every model this week ends in one decision about pipes
slides.text: Yanabi Water Authority Every model this week ends in one decision about pipes The question Dr. Nouran Al-Ateeq, director of asset management, must choose which of 140 districts to re-pipe or repair within a capital budget. The data Five years of reported bursts, 2021 to 2025, from networks of 1.2 km to 198 km. Synthetic, with known generating values. The difficulty A third of the districts recorded fewer than five bursts in five years, and most rural districts have no sensors. Day 1 builds the workflow on one model. Day 2 pools districts, Day 3 checks the models, Day 4 decides.

slides.title: Real asset and customer records stay out of a hosted notebook until classified
slides.text: From the pre-work Real asset and customer records stay out of a hosted notebook until classified The pre-work asked you to classify Yanabi's real burst and customer files under the national data classification levels. Burst counts per district: an internal record. Customer addresses on a burst ticket: personal data under the Personal Data Protection Law. This course uses only synthetic files, so Colab is allowed here. At work, the classification decides where a notebook may run. Ask Wurud first Wurud Al-Samhan, the data protection officer, signs off before a real extract leaves Yanabi's systems.

slides.text: Before the first lab One notebook proves your setup: run it now cd ds-401/labs uv sync uv run jupyter execute 00_setup_check.ipynb Or open 00_setup_check.ipynb in Colab and run all cells. It imports NumPyro, JAX and ArviZ, fits a tiny model and prints the versions. Everything runs on a laptop processor. No model is downloaded and no key is needed. AI policy. slides.title: Models that generate data
slides.text: Session 1 Models that generate data Write a generative model of burst counts with network length as exposure Compute a posterior on a grid from a prior and a likelihood Explain why the posterior of a small district leans on its prior 01

slides.title: You have fitted this count model before, by maximum likelihood
slides.text: Recap from DS-301 You have fitted this count model before, by maximum likelihood Counts with an exposure: log E[bursts] = log km + α + Xβ. The offset fixes the coefficient of log km at 1, so β describes a rate. Overdispersion and the negative binomial: Day 3 returns to them. What changes this week Each unknown gets a distribution, not one best value. The decision on Day 4 uses the whole distribution.

slides.title: Write the story that produces the bursts, then run it forwards
slides.text: A model is a simulator Write the story that produces the bursts, then run it forwards 1 · Rate bursts per km of main per year → 2 · Exposure times the district's km, for one year → 3 · Count a Poisson draw with that mean → 4 · Record what was reported (Day 2) If you can simulate the data, you can test every later step against a truth you chose.

slides.title: The posterior weighs every candidate rate by prior and data
slides.text: Prior times likelihood The posterior weighs every candidate rate by prior and data lp = log_prior(grid) + log_lik(grid, counts, km) w = np.exp(lp - lp.max()) w = w / w.sum() # posterior weights on the grid Work on the log scale: products of many probabilities underflow. Subtract the maximum before exponentiating. The normalising constant is the sum of the weights.

slides.title: Five years say little about a 1.2 km district
slides.text: Lab 1.1, task 4 Five years say little about a 1.2 km district District km Bursts, 5 years Median rate 90% interval D043, rural 1.2 2 0.194 0.058 to 0.523 D011, urban 198.0 87 0.087 0.073 to 0.104 Same prior, same five years: the small district's interval is 15 times wider, and its median still leans on the prior's centre.

slides.title: A grid works for one rate and fails for 140
slides.text: Why we need a sampler A grid works for one rate and fails for 140 10^280 grid points for 140 rates at 100 points each The grid grows exponentially with the number of unknowns. Almost all of its points have negligible posterior weight. A sampler spends its effort where the weight is: session 3.

slides.title: A Bayesian workflow is a loop, not a fit
slides.text: The week as a workflow A Bayesian workflow is a loop, not a fit Prior predictive Day 1 → Fit and diagnose Days 1 and 2 → Check and compare Day 3 → Calibrate the code Day 3 → Decide Day 4 A failed check sends you back. A model is expanded or replaced, and every step runs again.

slides.title: A narrow posterior
slides.text: Checkpoint A narrow posterior Two districts share the prior. District P has 200 km and 90 bursts in five years; district Q has 2 km and 3 bursts. Which statement about their posteriors holds? P's posterior depends more on the prior than Q's Q's posterior is wider and closer to the prior's centre Both have the same width because the prior is the same Q's posterior is narrow because 3 bursts is a small number

slides.title: A prior on the log rate means something only on the rate scale
slides.text: Reading a prior A prior on the log rate means something only on the rate scale Prior on the log rate 5th percentile Median 95th percentile N(0, 10), "flat-looking" 0.00000013 0.78 17,000,000 N(log 0.1, 1), weakly informative 0.019 0.10 0.52 N(log 0.5, 0.05), tight 0.46 0.50 0.54 Bursts per km of main per year, from 1,000 prior draws (Lab 1.2, task 1, quick run).

slides.title: The "harmless" flat prior predicts impossible district-years
slides.text: Lab 1.2, tasks 2 and 3 The "harmless" flat prior predicts impossible district-years 37% of simulated district-years above 500 bursts under N(0, 10) No district in the region has ever had 500 bursts in a year. With little data, such a prior pulls small districts towards absurd values. With a lot of data it hardly matters, which is how it hides.

slides.title: Simulate data from the prior alone, then ask an engineer
slides.text: Prior predictive simulation Simulate data from the prior alone, then ask an engineer 1 · Draw parameters from the prior → 2 · Simulate a year in all 140 districts → 3 · Compare with statements written before the data Not the burst counts. Tuning a prior to the observed data uses the data twice and makes the posterior too sure.

slides.title: A prior can also be wrong by being too sure
slides.text: The other failure A prior can also be wrong by being too sure Prior District-years above 500 Network totals in 300 to 3,000 N(0, 10) 37% 10% N(log 0.1, 1) 0% 73% N(log 0.5, 0.05) 0% 0% The vendor's tight prior never breaks the first statement, yet it rules out every network total the engineers call plausible.

slides.title: Every prior in the notebook carries one sentence of reason
slides.text: The evidence LO1 asks for Every prior in the notebook carries one sentence of reason α ~ Normal(log 0.1, 1) Centred on the engineers' "one burst per 10 km a year"; 73% of simulated network totals within their plausible range. β age ~ Normal(0, 0.5) Median rate ratio 1.0 per 10 years, 95th percentile 2.3: "might double, never five times". A reason quotes a number or a statement. "Weakly informative" alone is a label, not a reason.

slides.title: Weakly informative: rules out the impossible, stays open on the plausible
slides.text: A working definition Weakly informative: rules out the impossible, stays open on the plausible Too vague Puts weight on rates no pipe ever had. Harms small districts. Weakly informative Spans every rate an engineer would accept, and little beyond. Informative Carries a measurement: an audit, an earlier study. Day 2 uses one for reporting.

slides.title: Choosing the prior
slides.text: Checkpoint Choosing the prior A colleague sets the prior on the log burst rate by fitting it to the five years of observed counts, then fits the model to the same counts. What is the problem? Priors may never use data of any kind Nothing: with 700 counts the prior does not matter The data are used twice, so the posterior is too sure The sampler cannot handle a prior estimated from data

slides.title: Fitting with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
slides.text: Session 3 Fitting with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo Explain how Hamiltonian Monte Carlo uses the gradient of the log posterior Write a Poisson model with an offset in a probabilistic programming language Report rate ratios with posterior intervals 03

slides.title: A pile of posterior draws answers any question you can compute
slides.text: Monte Carlo A pile of posterior draws answers any question you can compute A median, an interval, a probability: functions of the draws. A derived quantity, such as next year's bursts in D017, is computed draw by draw. The decision on Day 4 is a cost computed in every draw, then averaged. mu = np.exp(a + b @ X[j]) * km[j] # one value per draw np.quantile(mu, [0.5, 0.05, 0.95])

slides.title: HMC rolls a particle across the posterior using its gradient
slides.text: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo HMC rolls a particle across the posterior using its gradient Position The current values of all parameters. Momentum A random push, drawn fresh at each iteration. Gradient The slope of the log posterior steers the path towards high density. The path is followed in small leapfrog steps; the end point is accepted or rejected so that the draws come from the posterior.

slides.title: NUTS chooses the path length; warm-up chooses the step size
slides.text: The No-U-Turn sampler NUTS chooses the path length; warm-up chooses the step size Setting Who sets it What goes wrong Path length NUTS: doubles the path until it turns back Paths that hit the maximum tree depth: slow Step size Warm-up: tuned to a target acceptance rate Too large for a curved region: divergences Mass matrix Warm-up: the scale of each parameter Very different scales: slow mixing

slides.title: The model is the generative story, written as code
slides.text: Lab 1.3, task 1 The model is the generative story, written as code def pooled_model(d, log_km, X, y=None): alpha = numpyro.sample("alpha", dist.Normal(np.log(0.10), 1.0)) beta = numpyro.sample("beta", dist.Normal(0.0, 0.5).expand([4]).to_event(1)) eta = alpha + X @ beta # log rate per district numpyro.sample("y", dist.Poisson(jnp.exp(log_km + eta[d])), obs=y) The same function simulates data when y is missing and conditions on it when y is given.

slides.title: The labs use NumPyro; the workflow is the same in every tool
slides.text: Probabilistic programming: interchangeable examples The labs use NumPyro; the workflow is the same in every tool Stan Through CmdStanPy or CmdStanR; compiles a model to C++. PyMC With Bambi for formula-style models. NumPyro On JAX; installs without a compiler, runs on a laptop or Colab. brms Formula models in R, fitted by Stan. Diagnostics and comparison: ArviZ in Python; loo and bayesplot in R. Your capstone may use any of them.

slides.text: Session 4 Reading the computation Read R-hat, bulk and tail effective sample size and divergences Tell an efficiency warning from a validity failure Judge when approximate inference is good enough for a question 04

slides.title: Four numbers decide whether a fit can be read
slides.text: Before reading any posterior Four numbers decide whether a fit can be read Diagnostic Course threshold, four chains What it detects Rank-normalised R-hat below 1.01 chains that disagree Bulk and tail ESS at least 400 too few independent draws for the centre or the tails Divergences zero, or explained regions the integrator could not follow E-BFMI above 0.3 momentum that cannot cross energy levels

slides.title: No divergence, and still one chain is somewhere else
slides.text: Fit C No divergence, and still one chain is somewhere else Chain Mean of α 1 -2.417 2 -2.411 3 -2.403 4 -1.229 1.60 R-hat of fit C

slides.title: 741 divergences: the sampler could not reach part of the posterior
slides.text: Fit B 741 divergences: the sampler could not reach part of the posterior A divergence is a path whose energy blew up: the step size was too large for the curvature there. The draws then miss that region, and every summary is biased. Fit B is the centred hierarchical model on the small districts: a funnel. Do not just raise target_accept. It shrinks the step size, often leaving fewer divergences and the same bias. Lab 2.3 changes the model instead.

slides.title: A capped tree costs time; it does not make the draws wrong
slides.text: Fit D A capped tree costs time; it does not make the draws wrong 33% of draws hit the tree-depth cap of 4 1.002 R-hat 1,452 smallest bulk ESS Zaina capped the tree depth to save time. The chains still mixed, so fit D can be read.

slides.title: Rank plots show chains that disagree better than trace plots do
slides.text: Looking at chains Rank plots show chains that disagree better than trace plots do Rank all draws of a parameter together, then plot each chain's ranks as a histogram. Chains from the same distribution: flat, similar histograms. A chain stuck high or low: a histogram piled at one end. pc = az.plot_rank(fits["fit_C"], var_names=["alpha", "tau"]) pc.savefig("artifacts/rank_fit_C.png")

slides.title: An approximation is fine when the posterior is simple and the question is its centre
slides.text: When approximate inference suffices An approximation is fine when the posterior is simple and the question is its centre 90% interval of β NUTS Variational (AutoNormal) Age per 10 years 0.265 to 0.334 0.253 to 0.326 Asbestos cement 0.533 to 0.699 0.551 to 0.698 Five parameters and 700 counts: close enough for a rate ratio. For 140 district effects, skewed spreads and tail decisions, sample.

slides.text: Checkpoint Which fit to send back A fit reports R-hat 1.003, bulk ESS 2,100, no divergences, and 40% of draws at the maximum tree depth. Another reports no divergences and R-hat 1.21. Which do you send back? The first, because 40% of trees are capped Neither, because neither has divergences Both, because each has a warning The second, because its chains disagree

slides.title: Before reading a fit
slides.text: Review of Day 1 Before reading a fit A colleague's fit reports R-hat 1.004 and bulk ESS 900, but 23 divergences. She wants to publish the rate ratios. What do you advise? Not yet: find where the divergences sit and change the model or its form, then refit Publish: R-hat and ESS are fine Run twice as many draws and publish Drop the divergent draws and publish the rest

slides.title: No, complete and partial pooling
slides.text: Session 1 No, complete and partial pooling Fit no-pooling, complete-pooling and partial-pooling models of the same counts Read shrinkage as a function of how much data a district has Check whether pooling pulls one group of districts towards another’s average 01

slides.title: You met random intercepts in DS-301; today they get priors and a defence
slides.text: Recap from DS-301 You met random intercepts in DS-301; today they get priors and a defence DS-301 Day 4 fitted random intercepts by maximum likelihood for 30 districts. Here: 140 districts, a prior on the spread τ, the whole posterior of every district. New today: predictors at the district level, the funnel, and measurement error. The question LO2 asks Not "is pooling allowed?" but "what does this pooling do to which districts, and can you defend it?"

slides.title: No pooling trusts each district; complete pooling trusts none
slides.text: Three ways to treat 140 districts No pooling trusts each district; complete pooling trusts none No pooling One rate per district, each from its own record. Tiny districts get wild estimates; 13 with no recorded burst look perfectly safe. Complete pooling One rate for all (Lab 1.3). Every district is average, including the old asbestos-cement ones. Partial pooling District rates drawn from a common distribution with spread τ. The data decide how much each district borrows.

slides.title: One line makes the districts a population
slides.text: Lab 2.1, task 1 One line makes the districts a population alpha = numpyro.sample("alpha", dist.Normal(np.log(0.10), 1.0)) tau = numpyro.sample("tau", dist.HalfNormal(0.5)) with numpyro.plate("district", J): eta = numpyro.sample("eta", dist.Normal(alpha, tau)) # the population numpyro.sample("y", dist.Poisson(jnp.exp(log_km + eta[d])), obs=y) τ near 0 is complete pooling; τ very large is no pooling. The posterior of τ chooses between them.

slides.title: Rural districts borrow most of their estimate; urban ones keep their own
slides.text: Lab 2.1, task 3 Rural districts borrow most of their estimate; urban ones keep their own Rural 0.55 Suburban 0.12 Urban 0.04 Median shrinkage towards the common rate (0: own estimate, 1: common rate). τ = 0.56, 90% interval 0.49 to 0.65 (quick run).

slides.title: Pooling towards one rate hides how much riskier the rural districts are
slides.text: Responsible use: Lab 2.1, task 4 Pooling towards one rate hides how much riskier the rural districts are 0.73 true gap of rural districts above the common rate (log scale) 0.11 the gap the estimates keep 16% of the real difference survives Who is harmed. Most kilometres are urban, so the common rate is an urban rate. A plan built on these estimates under-invests where the pipes are oldest.

slides.title: A defence of pooling says what it does to whom
slides.text: LO2's evidence A defence of pooling says what it does to whom Why partial pooling: 51 districts recorded fewer than five bursts; alone, their estimates are noise. What it does: small districts borrow from the population, here up to half their estimate. Whom it affects: the rural districts, whose risk it understates while one urban-dominated rate is the target. What changes next: shrink towards a prediction for each district's material and age.

slides.title: A district with no recorded burst
slides.text: Checkpoint A district with no recorded burst D120 is a rural district of 2 km with no burst recorded in five years. What does each model say about its rate? No pooling and complete pooling both give it a rate near zero Partial pooling gives it exactly the common rate No pooling: near zero; complete: the common rate; partial: between, close to the common rate No model can say anything until it has a burst

slides.title: Group-level predictors
slides.text: Session 2 Group-level predictors Add district-level predictors to the mean of a hierarchical model Compare the between-district spread before and after Explain why predictors change who is shrunk towards what 02

slides.title: Shrink each district towards what its pipes predict, not towards the average
slides.text: Group-level predictors Shrink each district towards what its pipes predict, not towards the average mu = alpha + X @ beta # material and age eta = mu + tau * z # district effect around it A rural asbestos-cement district of 40 years is now pulled towards the rate of such networks. τ now measures what material and age leave unexplained. The district-level predictors cost no data from the small districts: they are known for all 140.

slides.title: Material and age explain about half of what made districts differ
slides.text: Lab 2.2, task 3 Material and age explain about half of what made districts differ 0.56 τ without predictors 0.41 τ with material and age 47% of the variance between districts explained

slides.title: The predictors remove much of the rural bias, not all of it
slides.text: Lab 2.2, task 4 The predictors remove much of the rural bias, not all of it Mean log(estimate / true rate) Without predictors With material and age Rural -0.61 -0.25 Suburban -0.11 -0.12 Urban -0.06 -0.07 Rural estimates are still about 22% below the truth. Most rural districts have no sensors: session 4.

slides.title: A "rural" predictor fits the records better and the truth worse
slides.text: Lab 2.2, stretch A "rural" predictor fits the records better and the truth worse Its coefficient comes out negative: -0.21, 90% interval -0.48 to 0.04. It learns the low reported counts of rural districts, most without sensors. Rural estimates move further from their true rates: -0.32 on the log scale. A predictor that stands for a missing variable "Rural" here means "no sensors". Model the recording process instead (session 4).

slides.title: A good group-level predictor is known for every group and plausibly causal
slides.text: Choosing group-level predictors A good group-level predictor is known for every group and plausibly causal Material, age Known for all 140; engineering reasons to expect an effect. Pressure, soil Plausible; Yanabi has them for the urban districts only. A missing value is a modelling problem of its own. District kind Known for all, but stands for several things at once, including how bursts are recorded.

slides.title: What τ means now
slides.text: Checkpoint What τ means now After adding material and age, τ fell from 0.56 to 0.41. Nouran asks what that means for a rural asbestos-cement district with 3 recorded bursts. It is now pulled towards the rate predicted for old asbestos-cement networks, and somewhat more strongly It is pooled less because the model now knows more Its own three bursts no longer matter Its rate has fallen by 0.15

slides.title: The funnel and non-centred models
slides.text: Session 3 The funnel and non-centred models Recognise the funnel geometry behind divergences in a hierarchical model Rewrite a centred model in non-centred form Show that the repaired model gives a trustworthy answer 03

slides.title: When τ is small, every district effect must squeeze into a narrow neck
slides.text: Why fit B diverged When τ is small, every district effect must squeeze into a narrow neck The funnel of a centred hierarchical model η of one small district log τ divergences in the neck wide mouth: large τ Sketch. In Lab 2.3's run, every one of the centred model's 59 divergences had τ below its median.

slides.title: Non-centred: sample standard district effects, then scale them by τ
slides.text: Same model, different coordinates Non-centred: sample standard district effects, then scale them by τ eta = sample("eta", Normal(mu, tau)) z = sample("z", Normal(0, 1)) eta = deterministic("eta", mu + tau * z) The joint distribution is identical. In z, the posterior has no funnel: its shape no longer depends on τ.

slides.title: The non-centred model samples the 49 small districts cleanly
slides.text: Lab 2.3, task 4 The non-centred model samples the 49 small districts cleanly Divergences R-hat Bulk ESS E-BFMI Centred 59 1.037 49 0.10 Non-centred 0 1.004 563 0.82 Same priors, same 300 warm-up iterations, 2,000 kept draws (quick run).

slides.title: The centred fit missed the small values of τ
slides.text: Lab 2.3, task 5 The centred fit missed the small values of τ Centred 0.095 to 0.491 Non-centred 0.018 to 0.514 90% intervals of τ for the small districts. Missing small τ means pooling them less than the data allow.

slides.title: Raising target_accept removed the divergences and not the problem
slides.text: Lab 2.3, stretch Raising target_accept removed the divergences and not the problem 0 divergences at target_accept 0.99 1.144 R-hat, still far above 1.01 A smaller step reaches a little further into the neck, slowly. The chains still disagree, and τ's interval still starts at 0.061. Change the geometry; do not only shrink the step.

slides.title: With strong data in every group, the centred form can be the better one
slides.text: Not a rule of thumb With strong data in every group, the centred form can be the better one All 140 districts, centred No divergence, bulk ESS above 1,000 in Lab 2.1: large districts pin their own effects, so there is no funnel. 49 small districts, centred 59 divergences: little data per district, the prior's funnel dominates. Choose the form by the data, then check. The diagnostics, not a habit, decide.

slides.title: Under-reporting as measurement error

slides.title: The 2024 audit sets the prior the data cannot replace
slides.text: An informative prior, with its source The 2024 audit sets the prior the data cannot replace Ouda's team listened to 6 districts without sensors for a season: 28 of 40 bursts found had been reported. Beta(14, 6): mean 0.70, 90% interval 0.52 to 0.85; the audit at half weight. Half weight because six districts in one season may not represent all 76. The reason for this prior Cites a measurement, its size and why it was discounted: the standard of Day 1, applied to an informative prior.

slides.title: Posterior predictive checks

slides.title: A model that fits should be able to produce data like yours
slides.text: Posterior predictive checks A model that fits should be able to produce data like yours 1 · Draw parameters from the posterior → 2 · Replicate 700 district-years from the model with those parameters → 3 · Compare a statistic of the replicates with the same statistic of the data Choose the statistic for the decision. The total number of bursts fits almost any model; the variation from year to year decides how sure Day 4 can be.

slides.title: The Poisson model cannot produce the year-to-year variation Yanabi records
slides.text: Lab 3.1, task 2 The Poisson model cannot produce the year-to-year variation Yanabi records Districts over 10 km Observed Poisson replicates, 90% p Dispersion: variance of the five yearly counts over their mean 2.32 0.87 to 1.13 0.000 Share of district-years with no burst 0.048 0.021 to 0.050 0.12 The dispersion fails outright. The quiet years sit at the edge of the Poisson range without leaving it: not every statistic exposes a misfit.

slides.title: A negative binomial lets each year vary more than a Poisson
slides.text: Lab 3.1, task 3 A negative binomial lets each year vary more than a Poisson phi = numpyro.sample("phi", dist.Gamma(2.0, 0.2)) numpyro.sample("y", dist.NegativeBinomial2(mean, phi), obs=y) # variance = mean + mean**2 / phi φ = 7.0, 90% interval 5.6 to 9.0 (the generating value was 6). Both statistics now sit inside the replicates: p = 0.34 and 0.48. Weather, pressure surges and repair campaigns move a district's year; the Poisson has no room for them.

slides.title: A histogram of all district-years cannot tell the two models apart
slides.text: Lab 3.1, stretch A histogram of all district-years cannot tell the two models apart Observed counts against two models Poisson negative binomial bursts in a district-year (0 to 10) Square root of the frequencies, from the course's quick run. The dispersion within each district, 2.32 against Poisson replicates of 0.87 to 1.13, separates the same two models at once.

slides.title: Choosing a test statistic
slides.text: Checkpoint Choosing a test statistic Shabib proposes checking the Poisson model on the total number of bursts per year across the network. What do you tell him? The model was fitted to reproduce totals; check the variation within districts from year to year instead A good check: if the totals match, the model fits Checks are only valid on data the model has not seen If p is near 0.5 the model is proven correct

D3_1_expose_poisson_misfit.ipynb Replicated data from the Poisson model 6 min Share of zeros and dispersion 6 min Fit a negative binomial 6 min The same checks for the negative binomial 5 min A verdict in two sentences 2 min ✱ Stretch: Draw a rootogram of both models

slides.title: Comparing models by predictive accuracy
slides.text: Session 2 Comparing models by predictive accuracy Estimate expected log predictive density by Pareto-smoothed importance sampling Compare models by the difference and its standard error, not by the ranking alone Find influential observations from Pareto k and decide what to do about them 02

slides.title: Score each model on the district-years it did not see
slides.text: Comparing models by predictive accuracy Score each model on the district-years it did not see elpd : the expected log predictive density of a new district-year; higher is better. Leave-one-out refits 700 times; PSIS-LOO approximates all of them from one fit by importance sampling. Pareto k says, for each point, whether the approximation can be trusted (below about 0.7). Why not R² or the fit to the data Any model with more parameters fits the data it saw better. Predicting what it did not see is the fair contest.

slides.title: The negative binomial hierarchy predicts best, by far more than its error

slides.title: D017's 2023 is the year a trunk main failed: keep it, choose a model it does not overturn
slides.text: Lab 3.2, task 4 D017's 2023 is the year a trunk main failed: keep it, choose a model it does not overturn The Poisson hierarchy flags six district-years above 0.7, D017 in 2023 among them: 54 bursts against 18 to 27 in its other years. The negative binomial expects some unusual years: it flags one, at 0.71. Shabib confirms the failure. The year is real; deleting it would understate risk. A flagged point is a question Ask what happened before deciding what to do. An error is corrected; an event is modelled.

slides.title: Is the code right
slides.text: Session 3 Is the code right Recover known parameters from data simulated by the model Run a short simulation-based calibration and read its rank histograms Locate and fix an implementation error from the parameter that fails 03

slides.title: One successful recovery proves little
slides.text: Is the code right One successful recovery proves little A colleague simulated one dataset and recovered both parameters: α and β inside their 90% intervals. The model still has an error. One run passes by luck as easily as by being right. A correct model misses the truth 10% of the time; a wrong one can cover it often. Lab 3.3's starting point 20 northern districts, 445 km, a Poisson rate with an age effect. The simulator is right; one line of the model is not.

slides.title: If the code is right, the truth's rank among the draws is uniform
slides.text: Simulation-based calibration If the code is right, the truth's rank among the draws is uniform 1 · Simulate parameters from the prior, then data → 2 · Fit the model to those data: 99 draws → 3 · Rank count draws below the true value: 0 to 99 → 4 · Repeat 100 times; plot each parameter's ranks Shapes to read. Flat: right. U: posterior too narrow. Hump: too wide. Slope: biased.

slides.title: β's ranks pile up at both ends: its prior is five times too narrow
slides.text: Lab 3.3, tasks 3 to 5 β's ranks pile up at both ends: its prior is five times too narrow Share of ranks in the outer fifth (expected 20%) α β Colleague's model 33% (p = 0.09) 69% (p < 0.001) Fixed model 23% (p = 0.44) 25% (p = 0.66) beta = numpyro.sample("beta", dist.Normal(0.3, 0.2 ** 2)) # a variance where the scale belongs

slides.title: Calibration tests the code against the simulator, not the model against the world
slides.text: What calibration does not do Calibration tests the code against the simulator, not the model against the world It finds Coding errors, wrong parameterisations, a sampler that cannot fit the model. It misses The same mistake in both the simulator and the model; a model that is wrong about Yanabi. It costs 100 fits per calibration. Small models and short chains make it a few minutes on a laptop.

slides.title: Reading rank histograms
slides.text: Checkpoint Reading rank histograms In a calibration of 200 simulations, a parameter's ranks form a hump: few near 0 or 99, many in the middle. What does it say? The posterior is approximately normal, as expected The posterior is too narrow The posterior is too wide: the truth sits near its middle too often The sampler needs more warm-up

slides.title: The rubric
slides.text: How the repository is scored The rubric Model and priors 20% Computation 20% Checking 25% Decision 25% Reproducibility 10% Every claim carries a number from the run log. R-hat, divergences, a predictive p-value, an elpd difference with its standard error, an interval on the decision.

slides.title: 8 minutes to present, 7 to defend
slides.text: Format 8 minutes to present, 7 to defend 1 · Brief and model The decision maker's question; the structure and the priors you would defend. 2 · Evidence Diagnostics, the check that mattered, the comparison of models. 3 · Decision The choice, its interval, the remaining risk, what more data is worth. The questions. The assessor changes one prior or one cost; you predict the effect on the decision, then rerun. Then your peer asks the question from their review of your model.

slides.title: Predict in words first, then check with the model

Then the rerun. Weak "The results should be robust." Or: rerunning before saying anything, then describing what changed.
